title: Rosh Hashanah: Hannah (1 Samuel 1)
hook: the haftarah tells of Hannah praying for a child, and being heard
tomorrow: Rosh Hashanah: the boy is heard (Genesis 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three sounds of the shofar. Your line was a sigh and a sob. Today, a woman the rabbis learned to pray from, read on the new year.

Every year the family goes up to the sanctuary at Shiloh for a festive meal, and every year it's the same scene. Elkanah gives portions of meat to his wife Peninnah and all her sons and daughters. To his other wife, Hannah, whom he loves, he gives a double portion, because Hannah has no children. And every year, Peninnah makes sure she feels it. Hannah cries and won't eat. Her husband asks, gently and a bit cluelessly: "am not I better to thee than ten sons?"
screen: `EVERY YEAR, UP TO SHILOH.` → `A DOUBLE PORTION, NO CHILDREN.` → `BETTER THAN TEN SONS?`

segments.voice: This is the haftarah, the prophetic reading, for the first day of Rosh Hashanah: the first chapter of Samuel. Weeks ago you met Hannah's quiet prayer, lips moving with no voice, which the rabbis made the model for the Amidah. Today's question is why her story is read on the new year. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 11a, says that on Rosh Hashanah three women were remembered: Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, three women who had longed for children. So on the day the liturgy is full of remembrance, the reading is about a woman who asked to be remembered, almost in those words. Her vow says: if Thou wilt "remember me, and not forget Thy handmaid." Watch what Hannah does. She doesn't argue with Peninnah, and she doesn't accept her husband's comfort as an answer. She gets up from the table, goes to the sanctuary, and pours out her soul. When the priest Eli thinks she's drunk, she corrects him, respectfully and firmly, and he blesses her. The text says her face was no more sad. Before anything has changed, she's already lighter. In time she has a son, Samuel, and here's the turn: she gives him back, bringing him to serve at Shiloh. The next chapter is her song of thanks, about reversals: the Lord brings low and lifts up, the barren bears seven. Being heard, for Hannah, began before the answer came. It began with being seen.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY'S HAFTARAH.` · `SARAH, RACHEL AND HANNAH.` · `REMEMBER ME, AND NOT FORGET.` · `HER FACE WAS NO MORE SAD.` · then, large: `HANNAH WAS HEARD.`

segments.voice: Let yourself name something you long for, not a small want but something you've carried, maybe for years, maybe quietly, the way Hannah got up from the table and named hers. If you pray, pour it out to God in your own words, lips moving if you like; if not, say it to yourself honestly, without needing an answer. Notice whether naming it changes how you sit.
Rosh Hashanah. The new year, when the first day's reading tells of Hannah, remembered and heard.
Your line: Hannah was heard. Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, remembered on this day. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 647 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ROSH HASHANAH: THE BOY IS HEARD (GENESIS 21).`

howItsDone: On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, after the Torah reading, the haftarah from 1 Samuel 1:1–2:10 is chanted in the synagogue, including Hannah's prayer and her song of thanks.

chat.says: Why read a story about Hannah wanting a child on Rosh Hashanah?
options: The Talmud says Hannah was remembered on this day, and she asked to be remembered.
It's read because Peninnah, her rival, was remembered on that day too.
It's read because her husband Elkanah was the one remembered that day.
chat.meaning: Rosh Hashanah 11a says Sarah, Rachel and Hannah were remembered on Rosh Hashanah, and Hannah's vow asks God to remember her.
